The clockmaker's shop had emptied over the years, its shelves surrendering one timepiece after another to collectors and tourists. Only the grandfather clock remained, standing in the corner like a patient sentinel, its brass pendulum swinging with the steadiness of a heartbeat.

"Name your price," the man said, third visitor that week.

Elsie shook her head, polishing the clock's walnut case with a cloth gone soft from decades of use. "It's not for sale."

"It's the last one. Surely—"

"My husband built it the winter before he died." She wound the key, listening to the gears take up their familiar song. "Every clock I ever sold, I sold gladly. But this one doesn't tell time. It tells *our* time. The christening of my daughter. The night the lights went out across the valley. Forty years of midnights."

The man left without another word.

Elsie sat beside the clock, and together they kept counting.
